topics.title: Number Systems & Logic Levels
topics.content:
Number Systems:
- Binary (Base-2): Uses 0 and 1. Positional values are powers of 2.
- Octal (Base-8): Uses digits 0-7. Group binary bits in sets of 3.
- Hexadecimal (Base-16): Uses 0-9 and A-F (A=10...F=15). Group binary bits in sets of 4.

Logic Levels:
- Digital systems work with two distinct voltage levels: Logic 0 (LOW/FALSE, ~0V) and Logic 1 (HIGH/TRUE, ~+5V or +3.3V).
- Positive Logic: Higher voltage = 1, Lower voltage = 0.
- Negative Logic: Higher voltage = 0, Lower voltage = 1.

topics.title: Logic Gates & Truth Tables
topics.content:
Fundamental logic gate operations:
- AND: Y = A · B (Output 1 only when ALL inputs are 1)
- OR: Y = A + B (Output 1 when AT LEAST ONE input is 1)
- NOT (Inverter): Y = A' (Output is opposite of input)
- NAND: Y = (A · B)' (Universal gate; output 0 only when all inputs are 1)
- NOR: Y = (A + B)' (Universal gate; output 1 only when all inputs are 0)
- XOR: Y = A ⊕ B (Output 1 when inputs are DIFFERENT; A ⊕ A = 0, A ⊕ 0 = A)
- XNOR: Y = (A ⊕ B)' (Output 1 when inputs are the SAME; equality checker)

topics.title: Boolean Algebra & De Morgan's Theorems
topics.content:
Basic Laws:
- Identity: A + 0 = A, A · 1 = A
- Null: A + 1 = 1, A · 0 = 0
- Idempotent: A + A = A, A · A = A
- Complement: A + A' = 1, A · A' = 0
- Involution: (A')' = A

De Morgan's Theorems:
1. (A + B)' = A' · B'
2. (A · B)' = A' + B'

Absorption & Consensus Laws:
- Absorption: A + A·B = A, A · (A + B) = A
- Consensus Theorem: A·B + A'·C + B·C = A·B + A'·C

topics.title: SOP, POS Forms and K-Maps
topics.content:
Sum-of-Products (SOP):
- Sum (OR) of Product (AND) terms (minterms).
- Focuses on rows where output = 1. Variable = 1 → A, Variable = 0 → A'.

Product-of-Sums (POS):
- Product (AND) of Sum (OR) terms (maxterms).
- Focuses on rows where output = 0. Variable = 0 → A, Variable = 1 → A'.

Karnaugh Map (K-Map):
- Visual tool for Boolean simplification using Gray Code ordering (00, 01, 11, 10).
- Cells arranged so adjacent cells differ by only 1 bit.
- Group 1s (SOP) or 0s (POS) in powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16). Groups can wrap around edges.

topics.title: Multiplexers and Demultiplexers
topics.content:
Multiplexer (MUX):
- Data selector that routes 1 of 2ⁿ inputs to 1 output using n select lines.
- Boolean Expression (4-to-1 MUX): Y = S₁'S₀'I₀ + S₁'S₀I₁ + S₁S₀'I₂ + S₁S₀I₃
- Universal logic element (can implement any Boolean function).

Demultiplexer (DEMUX):
- Data distributor that routes 1 input to 1 of 2ⁿ outputs using n select lines.

topics.title: Decoders and Encoders
topics.content:
Decoders and Encoders:
- Decoder: Converts n input lines into 2ⁿ unique output lines (minterms). Act as DEMUX when driven with an Enable line.
- Encoder: Converts 2ⁿ input lines into an n-bit binary code.
- Priority Encoder: Resolves conflicts when multiple inputs are active simultaneously by honoring the highest-priority input.

topics.title: Binary Adders and Subtractors
topics.content:
Half Adder: Adds 2 bits (A, B). Sum = A ⊕ B, Carry = A · B
Full Adder: Adds 3 bits (A, B, C_in). Sum = A ⊕ B ⊕ C_in, C_out = AB + BC_in + AC_in

Half Subtractor: Subtracts 2 bits (A - B). Diff = A ⊕ B, Borrow = A'B
Full Subtractor: Subtracts 3 bits (A - B - B_in). Diff = A ⊕ B ⊕ B_in, B_out = A'B + A'B_in + BB_in

Ripple Carry Adder: Chain of Full Adders where Carry out ripples to the next stage C_in.

topics.title: Signed Numbers & 2's Complement
topics.content:
Representation Methods:
- Sign-Magnitude: MSB is sign bit (0 = +, 1 = -). Two representations of zero (+0, -0).
- 1's Complement: Invert all bits. Two representations of zero (+0, -0).
- 2's Complement: Invert all bits and add 1. Only ONE representation of zero (0000). Range for n bits: -2ⁿ⁻¹ to +(2ⁿ⁻¹ - 1).

Overflow Detection in 2's Complement:
- Occurs when Carry-into MSB ≠ Carry-out of MSB.
- Alternatively: Adding two positive numbers yields a negative result, or adding two negative numbers yields a positive result.

topics.title: Flip-Flops and Latches
topics.content:
RS Flip-Flop: Basic memory element. S=1 sets Q=1, R=1 resets Q=0. S=R=1 is forbidden/invalid.
JK Flip-Flop: Eliminates invalid state. J=1, K=1 causes output to TOGGLE.
D Flip-Flop: Data delay flip-flop; transfers D input to Q output on clock edge.
T Flip-Flop: Toggle flip-flop (J=K=T). T=1 toggles output; T=0 holds output (Q_next = T ⊕ Q).
Master-Slave Flip-Flop: Two flip-flops in series (master captures on clock high, slave updates on clock low). Eliminates race-around conditions.

topics.title: Registers & Shift Register Applications
topics.content:
Types of Shift Registers:
- PIPO (Parallel-In Parallel-Out): Fast parallel storage.
- SISO (Serial-In Serial-Out): Used for time delay lines and serial data transmission.
- SIPO (Serial-In Parallel-Out): Serial-to-parallel conversion.
- PISO (Parallel-In Serial-Out): Parallel-to-serial conversion.
- Universal / Bidirectional: Can shift left, right, load, or hold via mode lines.

Counters derived from shift registers:
- Ring Counter: Circular shift register; n-bit gives n states.
- Johnson Counter (Twisted Ring): Complemented output fed back; n-bit gives 2n states.

topics.title: Asynchronous and Synchronous Counters
topics.content:
Asynchronous (Ripple) Counters:
- Flip-flops do NOT share the same clock; each stage is clocked by previous stage output.
- Subject to propagation delay and decoding glitches.
- Modulus: n-bit counter counts 2ⁿ states (Mod-8, Mod-16). Mod-N (Decade) uses reset logic (e.g., NAND gate detecting 1010 to reset Mod-10).

Synchronous Counters:
- All flip-flops share the SAME clock simultaneously.
- Higher speed with no cumulative ripple delay.

topics.title: Microprocessor Basics & Architecture
topics.content:
Microprocessor vs Microcontroller:
- Microprocessor contains only the CPU (e.g., 8085, 8086), needing external memory and I/O.
- Microcontroller integrates CPU, memory, and I/O on a single chip (e.g., 8051, PIC).

Functions: Fetch → Decode → Execute → Store.

topics.title: Intel 8085 Microprocessor Architecture
topics.content:
Features: 8-bit architecture, 16-bit address bus (64KB memory), 3 MHz clock, single +5V supply, 40 pins.
- General Purpose Registers: B, C, D, E, H, L (16-bit register pairs: BC, DE, HL for memory addressing).
- Accumulator (A): 8-bit register for ALU operations.
- Flag Register (PSW): 5 active flags: Sign (S), Zero (Z), Auxiliary Carry (AC - set when carry moves from bit 3 to bit 4), Parity (P), Carry (CY).
- 16-bit Registers: Program Counter (PC) holds next instruction address; Stack Pointer (SP) points to top of stack.
- Hardware Interrupts: TRAP (non-maskable, highest priority, vector 0024H), RST 7.5, RST 6.5, RST 5.5, INTR (lowest priority, maskable).
- Control Signals: ALE (Address Latch Enable separates address/data on multiplexed AD7-AD0), RD, WR, IO/M.

topics.title: 8085 Instruction Length & Addressing Modes
topics.content:
Instruction Bytes / Length:
- 1-Byte Instructions: Opcode only (e.g., MOV A, B -> 78H).
- 2-Byte Instructions: Opcode + 8-bit data/address (e.g., MVI A, 32H -> 3E 32).
- 3-Byte Instructions: Opcode + 16-bit address/data stored in Little-Endian format (e.g., LDA 2050H -> 3A 50 20).

Addressing Modes:
- Immediate (MVI A, 25H), Register (MOV A, B), Direct (LDA 2050H), Indirect (MOV A, M where M is [HL]), Implicit (CMA).

topics.title: Intel 8086 Microprocessor Architecture
topics.content:
Features: 16-bit architecture, 20-bit address bus (1MB memory space), 6-byte instruction queue, 5-10 MHz clock.
Two-Unit Architecture (Pipelining):
1. Bus Interface Unit (BIU): Fetches instructions, calculates physical address, maintains 6-byte instruction FIFO queue. Segment Registers (16-bit each): CS, DS, SS, ES.
   - Physical Address Calculation = Segment × 16 + Offset (or Segment << 4 + Offset).
2. Execution Unit (EU): Decodes and executes instructions. Registers: AX (Accumulator), BX (Base), CX (Count), DX (Data), SP, BP, SI, DI.
   - Flags: 9 flags (6 Status: CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF; 3 Control: DF, IF, TF).
Operating Modes: Minimum mode (MN/MX = 1, single processor) and Maximum mode (MN/MX = 0, multiprocessor with 8288 bus controller).
Memory Banks: 1MB divided into Even Bank (A0 = 0, BHE) and Odd Bank (A0 = 1, BLE) for 16-bit word alignment.

topics.title: 8086 Addressing Modes & Instruction Set
topics.content:
Addressing Modes:
- Immediate (MOV AX, 1234H), Register (MOV AX, BX), Direct (MOV AX, [2050H]), Register Indirect (MOV AX, [BX]), Based (MOV AX, [BX+5]), Indexed (MOV AX, [SI+10]), Based Indexed (MOV AX, [BX+SI]), Based Indexed with Displacement (MOV AX, [BX+SI+10]).

Instruction Categories:
- Data Transfer: MOV, PUSH, POP, IN, OUT, LEA, LDS, LES.
- Arithmetic: ADD, ADC, SUB, SBB, INC, DEC, MUL, IMUL, DIV, IDIV, NEG.
- Logical & Bit Manipulation: AND, OR, XOR, NOT, TEST, CMP, SHL, SHR, SAL, SAR, ROL, ROR, RCL, RCR.
- Control Transfer: JMP, JZ, JNZ, JC, JNC, JE, JNE, CALL, RET, LOOP.
- String Operations: MOVSB, CMPSB, SCASB, LODSB, STOSB (uses REP prefix).

topics.title: Assembly Language Programming Basics
topics.content:
Structure: [Label:] Mnemonic [Operands] [;Comment]
Assembler Directives: ORG (Origin), END, DB (Define Byte), DW (Define Word), EQU (Equate), SEGMENT/ENDS, ASSUME.

topics.title: Memory Classification and Interfacing
topics.content:
Memory Hierarchy: Registers → Cache (SRAM) → Main Memory (DRAM) → Secondary Storage (HDD/SSD) → Tertiary Storage (Magnetic Tapes).
Memory Types: Volatile (SRAM, DRAM) vs Non-Volatile (Mask ROM, PROM, EPROM - erased using UV light, EEPROM/Flash).
Buses: Address Bus (Unidirectional), Data Bus (Bidirectional), Control Bus.
Interfacing Methods:
- Memory-Mapped I/O: I/O devices share address space with memory; accessed using standard memory instructions.
- I/O-Mapped I/O (Isolated I/O): Uses separate address space for I/O devices using IN and OUT instructions.

topics.title: Programmable Peripheral Interface (Intel 8255 PPI)
topics.content:
Features: 24 I/O pins configured in three 8-bit ports (Port A, Port B, Port C).
Modes of Operation:
- Mode 0: Simple I/O (no handshaking).
- Mode 1: Strobed I/O (uses Port C pins for handshaking signals).
- Mode 2: Bidirectional I/O (Port A bidirectional with handshaking).

topics.title: Serial Communication & Standards
topics.content:
Transmission Types:
- Synchronous: Block transmission synchronized with a shared clock signal.
- Asynchronous: Byte-by-byte transmission using Start bit (logic 0) and Stop bit(s) (logic 1). Baud rate refers to signal changes/symbols per second.

Standards:
- RS-232: Short distance serial standard (+3V to +15V for Logic 0, -3V to -15V for Logic 1).
- RS-422 / RS-485: Differential signaling for long distances and multi-drop networks.
- USB: Modern high-speed serial interface.

topics.title: Direct Memory Access (DMA)
topics.content:
Concept: Allows high-speed data transfer directly between memory and I/O devices without continuous CPU intervention.
Operation:
- DMA Controller (Intel 8237, 4 channels) sends HOLD request to CPU.
- CPU releases system buses and responds with HLDA (HOLD Acknowledge).
- Transfer Modes: Single Transfer, Block Transfer, Demand Transfer.

topics.title: Interrupt Basics & Service Routine (ISR)
topics.content:
Concept: An interrupt signal temporarily pauses CPU execution to perform an urgent task via an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR).
Types: Hardware (Maskable/Non-Maskable), Software (INT n), Internal Exceptions (Divide by zero, Overflow).
Processing Sequence:
1. Complete current instruction.
2. Push Flags, CS, and IP onto stack.
3. Fetch ISR address from Interrupt Vector Table (IVT).
4. Execute ISR code.
5. Return via IRET instruction (pops IP, CS, Flags in 8086; 8085 uses RET).

topics.title: Interrupt Vector Table & Controller (8259 PIC)
topics.content:
Interrupt Vector Table (IVT):
- Located at 00000H - 003FFH in 8086 memory map.
- Holds 256 vector pointers (4 bytes each: CS and IP). Vector Address = Interrupt Type × 4.

Intel 8259 PIC:
- Manages up to 8 hardware interrupt lines (IR0-IR7), expandable up to 64 via cascading.
- Resolves priority among simultaneous requests and passes vector to CPU.

questions.question: The binary equivalent of (25)₁₀ is:
questions.explanation: 25 in binary is 16 + 8 + 1 = 11001₂.

questions.question: Which gate gives output 1 only when all inputs are 1?
questions.explanation: An AND gate outputs HIGH (1) only when all of its inputs are HIGH (1).

questions.question: De Morgan's law states that (A + B)' is equal to:
questions.explanation: De Morgan's first theorem states that the complement of a sum equals the product of the complements: (A+B)' = A'·B'.

questions.question: A 4×1 MUX has how many select lines?
questions.explanation: 2ⁿ = 4 inputs requires n = 2 select lines.

questions.question: The 2's complement of (1010)₂ is:
questions.explanation: 1's complement of 1010 is 0101. Adding 1 gives 0110.

questions.question: In a JK Flip-Flop, if J=1, K=1, and clock rises, the output will:
questions.explanation: When both J and K are 1, the JK flip-flop operates in toggle mode.

questions.question: A 4-bit shift register can store:
questions.explanation: An n-bit shift register contains n flip-flops and can store n bits.

questions.question: Which register is used by default for multiplication/division in 8086?
questions.explanation: The AX accumulator register is implicitly used in MUL and DIV instructions.

questions.question: Which memory level in the memory hierarchy is fastest?
questions.explanation: Cache memory (SRAM) is faster than main memory (RAM) and secondary storage.

questions.question: The first step in CPU interrupt processing is:
questions.explanation: Upon acknowledging an interrupt, the CPU first saves its state (Flags, CS, IP) onto the stack.

questions.question: The decimal equivalent of (1101.101)₂ is:
The hexadecimal equivalent of (10101100)₂ is:
questions.explanation: Grouping 4 bits: 1010₂ = A, 1100₂ = C. Result = AC₁₆.

questions.question: The 1's complement of (10110)₂ is:
questions.explanation: Inverting each bit of 10110 gives 01001.

questions.question: The Boolean expression A + A'B simplifies to:
questions.explanation: Using distributive law: A + A'B = (A + A')(A + B) = 1 · (A + B) = A + B.

questions.question: The minimum number of 2-input NAND gates required to implement XOR (A ⊕ B) is:
questions.explanation: An XOR function requires exactly 4 NAND gates to build.

questions.question: The K-map for F(A,B,C) = ∑(0,2,4,6) simplifies to:
questions.explanation: Minterms 0,2,4,6 correspond to all cells where C = 0, which simplifies to C'.

questions.question: Which logic gate is considered universal?
questions.explanation: NAND (and NOR) are universal gates because any logic function can be implemented using only them.

questions.question: The output of an XOR gate is 1 when:
questions.explanation: XOR produces 1 when the inputs differ from each other.

questions.question: A 16:1 Multiplexer requires how many select lines?
questions.explanation: 2⁴ = 16, so 4 select lines are needed.

questions.question: A 3-to-8 decoder has how many outputs?
questions.explanation: An n-to-2ⁿ decoder with 3 input lines produces 2³ = 8 output lines.

questions.question: The full adder circuit has:
questions.explanation: Full adder accepts 3 inputs (A, B, C_in) and outputs 2 bits (Sum, C_out).

questions.question: A 4-bit binary adder can add unsigned numbers up to a maximum decimal sum of:
questions.explanation: Max value for 4 bits is 2⁴ - 1 = 15.

questions.question: Race-around condition occurs in which flip-flop when level-triggered?
questions.explanation: In level-triggered JK FF with J=1, K=1, output toggles continuously during clock high period.

questions.question: The output frequency of a MOD-10 counter with a 1 kHz input clock is:
questions.explanation: Output frequency = Input clock / MOD number = 1000 Hz / 10 = 100 Hz.

questions.question: The minimum number of flip-flops needed for a MOD-16 counter is:
questions.explanation: 2ⁿ ≥ 16 → n = 4 flip-flops.

questions.question: A master-slave flip-flop is used to eliminate:
questions.explanation: Master-slave structure prevents multiple toggles within a single clock pulse.

questions.question: In 8086, if the address bus has 20 lines, the maximum memory capacity is:
questions.explanation: 2²⁰ bytes = 1,048,576 bytes = 1 MB.

questions.question: In 8086, the physical memory address is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Physical address = (Segment Register << 4) + Offset = Segment × 16 + Offset.

questions.question: The size of the instruction prefetch queue in 8086 BIU is:
questions.explanation: 8086 BIU maintains a 6-byte instruction queue for pipelining.

questions.question: In memory-mapped I/O:
options: I/O devices use separate address space
I/O devices share address space with memory
Only 256 I/O devices can be connected
questions.explanation: In memory-mapped I/O, I/O devices are assigned addresses within the memory address map.

questions.question: Intel 8255 PPI has how many I/O ports?
questions.explanation: 8255 PPI contains three 8-bit ports: Port A, Port B, and Port C.

questions.question: When the DMA controller requires the system bus, it sends which signal to the CPU?
questions.explanation: The DMA controller asserts the HOLD line to request system bus control.

questions.question: Which of the following is a non-maskable hardware interrupt in 8086?
questions.explanation: NMI (Non-Maskable Interrupt) cannot be disabled by software via the Interrupt Flag.

questions.question: In 8086, each entry in the Interrupt Vector Table (IVT) occupies:
questions.explanation: Each vector requires 4 bytes (2 bytes for IP, 2 bytes for CS).

questions.question: The instruction used to return control from an Interrupt Service Routine in 8086 is:
questions.explanation: IRET pops IP, CS, and the Flags register from the stack to resume original execution.

questions.question: Which 8085 interrupt has the highest priority and is non-maskable?
questions.explanation: TRAP is the highest-priority non-maskable hardware interrupt in 8085.

questions.question: In 8085, the Auxiliary Carry (AC) flag is set when a carry is generated from:
questions.explanation: AC flag is set during arithmetic/BCD operations when a carry occurs from bit 3 (lower nibble) to bit 4.

questions.question: The length of the instruction 'LDA 2050H' in 8085 is:
questions.explanation: LDA 2050H requires 3 bytes: 1 byte for opcode (3AH), 1 byte for low-order address (50H), and 1 byte for high-order address (20H).

questions.question: Direct Memory Access (DMA) transfer is faster because:
options: Data is transferred directly between memory and I/O without CPU intervention
questions.explanation: DMA allows peripherals to directly read/write memory without making the CPU fetch and execute byte-by-byte transfer instructions.

questions.question: Baud rate in serial communication refers to the number of:
options: Signal changes or symbols per second
questions.explanation: Baud rate is defined as the unit of signaling speed equal to the number of discrete signal changes per second.
